notes.text: Rent — A metaphor taken from men, that when they would resolutely help one in distress, break and fling open doors and whatever may hinder. Flow down - That all impediments might be removed out of the way: possibly an allusion to God's coming down upon Mount Sinai, in those terrible flames of fire.

Fire — Come with such zeal for thy people, that the solid mountains may be no more before thy breath, than metal that runs, or water that boils by the force of a vehement fire. Known - That thine enemies may know thy power, and that thy name may be dreaded among them.

Terrible things — This may relate to what he did among the Egyptians, tho' it be not recorded, and afterward in the wilderness. Looked not for - Such things as we could never expect. Mountains - Kings, princes, and potentates, may metaphorically be understood by these mountains.

Besides thee — This is to be applied to all the wonderful works, that God at all times wrought for his people: and thus they are a plea with God, that they might well expect such things from him now, that had done such wonderful things for their fathers. Waiteth - This may be taken with reference both to the state of grace and glory, those incomprehensible things that are exhibited through Christ in the mysteries of the gospel.
Meetest — As the father the prodigal. Worketh - That rejoices to work righteousness. Continuance - To those that work righteousness. Be saved - In so doing, in working righteousness.

Unclean — Formerly there were some that feared thee; but now we are all as one polluted mass, nothing of good left in us by reason of an universal degeneracy. And all - The very best of us all are no better than the uncleanest things. Taken - Carried away to Babylon, as leaves hurried away by a boisterous wind.
That calleth — That call upon thee as they ought. Take hold - Either to stay thee from departing from us, or to fetch thee back when departed.
Our father — Notwithstanding all this thou art our father both by creation, and by adoption, therefore pity us thy children.
Thy people — Thou hast no people in covenant but us, and wilt thou not leave thyself a people in the world?

glossa.text: *O that thou wouldst rend.* ((HIER.)) In his own person, etc., *as far as* likewise David: *He bowed the heavens, and came down ((Psal. XVII))*.

*The waters should burn. ((SYM.)) The waters of the sea should burn with fire.* Which is, that the peoples of the world should be inflamed with the fire of charity. Whence: *I am come to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I but that it burn? ((Luc. XII.))* and so *thy name should be made known,* which is Christ Jesus, *to thy enemies,* namely to the Jews.

*We shall not bear it.* We Jews, but we shall blaspheme, saying: *By Beelzebub the prince of devils he casteth out devils ((Matth. XII))* . For the prophet says this in the person of unbelie

*Thou camest down.* As though, his prayers having been heard, he says: *Thou camest down,* etc. [1308C] *The mountains.* Their power lost: *Now shall the prince of this world be cast out [n: (Joan. XII)]*. And to the Jews it is said: *The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you [n: (Matth. XXI)]*, namely Holy Scripture and all glory and all dignity.

*From the beginning of the world.* Hence Paul, writing to the Corinthians, takes his testimony, not word for word, but expressing the sense. *The eye.* Because it is not a body or a colour. What the Apostle sets down, *it hath not ascended into the heart of man*, because it is greater, and the heart ought to be directed thither. For he prepared his very self, the knowledge of himself, the knowledge of the holy Trinity; whence: *This is eternal life, that they may know thee the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent ((Joan. XVII))* . Him no one can see; whence that: *No man hath ever seen God ((Joan. I))*.
*Behold thou,* etc. In the person of the unbelieving people, who, wishing to pass over to the truth of the Gospel, put forward with the mouth a penance which he had not in the heart.

*Of a menstruous woman,* etc. *Mene* in Hebrew, *luna* in Latin; whence *menstruatae*, women who each several month are wont to endure a flux of blood. And then men ought to abstain from them. For then are conceived those condemned in their members, the blind, the lame, the leprous and the like: so that, because the parents were not ashamed to be mingled in the bedchamber, their sins may lie open to all, and be openly reproved in their little ones. *Wind.* A motion of the air, as there, *He commanded the winds and the sea ((Matth. VIII))*. Or the Holy Spirit: *Of a vehement Spirit coming (Act I)*. For here *Spirit* is put for wind, with the signification of the Holy Spirit. Or, the temptation of demons and of evil men, as that: *The floods came, and the winds blew ((Matth. VII))*: and this is as it were a wind.

*And now, O Lord.* As if he should say: If we consider our own merits, we must despair; if thy clemency, who scourgest every son whom thou receivest, we dare to pour out prayers, for thou art our father. *The works of thy hands.* As if he should say: Look upon thy work, not upon our merits. The right confession of the mystery of the Trinity is the ignorance of knowledge.

*Be not angry, O Lord.* This is, we do not shun wrath, nor do we further seek that patience through which we treasure up to ourselves wrath in the day of vengeance: but we beseech that thou be not angry with us enough, that is, that thou remember not our iniquity in the time of vengeance.

notes.text: Joseph — The children of Joseph or Israel. The name of Joseph, the most eminent of the patriarchs, is elsewhere put for all the tribes. Cherubim - Which were by the mercy seat above the ark.

Before Ephraim — Here is an allusion to the ancient situation of the tabernacle in the wilderness, where these tribes were placed on the west-side of the tabernacle, in which the ark was, which consequently was before them.
Turn us — To thy self.

Be — To protect and strengthen him. Right-hand - Benjamin signifies the son of the right hand, a dearly beloved son, as Benjamin was to Jacob. Son of man - The people of Israel, who are often spoken of as one person, as God's son and first-born.

Go back — Revolt from thee to idolatry or wickedness. Quicken - Revive and restore us to our tranquility. This psalm may assist us in our solemn feast-days, in praising God, for what he is, and what he has done, ver. 1-7. In admonishing one another, concerning our obligations to God, the danger of revolting from him, and the happiness of keeping close to him, ver. 8-16. To the chief musician upon Gittith, A psalm of Asaph.

glossa.text: *Thou that rulest,* etc. ((AUG.)) Here Asaph, enlightened, speaks of the coming of Christ, who converts man, and makes firm the vineyard brought out of Egypt: this is the testimony for them that are changed. ((CASS.)) Above he was fearful, who was praying for the sins of the Synagogue: now he presumes, and to those changed for the better he gives a testimony. This psalm is the testimony of the Synagogue concerning the head himself, and his body. ((ID.)) A prayer for the first coming, through which the reparation of the human race is made. ((ID.)) Being finished, he makes an end. O God, O Son. *Thou that rulest,* spiritually, *Israel,* who see thee, *Give ear,* that is, pour the light of goodness upon us, that we may be bright from thee, who of ourselves are dark. *Joseph.* ((ID.)) Thou leadest the faithful people into the folds of God, as sheep to the pastures, of whom: *And other sheep I have that are not of this fold, and them I must bring, that there may be one fold and one shepherd ((Joan. X))*. Each has its own proper word: Israel *is ruled,* Joseph *is led,* that is, the devout people. *Be made manifest.* ((ID.)) He asks that he who was in the secret of majesty may appear before the Jews through the incarnation, as it had been promised, working in them these powers which are signified by these names, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasse. ((AUG.)) *Be made manifest before.* Known to the angels, be made known to men.

*Before Ephraim.* ((AUG.)) That is, in the nation of the Jews, where these tribes are, namely before fruitfulness, and before the son of the right hand, that we also may be the fulness of knowledge through charity, which is God; and before Manasse, that is, the forgotten one, that thou mayest now come into his mind, according to that saying: *All the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted.* ((ID.)) *Stir up.* He repeats, etc., *as far as* crucified through weakness, rise again through power. ((CASS.)) *Stir up thy power* of miracles, etc., *as far as* whence: *God is faithful, who suffereth you not to be tempted above that which you are able,* etc. ((I Cor. X)).

*Thy face.* ((AUG.)) This face was veiled to Asaph in the time of the weakness of Christ, and then Asaph was sick, not being able to look upon him veiled with a cloud: of which it is said: *God ascended upon a light cloud,* and he shall enter, or shall go into, Egypt, that is, flesh free from sin; but he enlightened it when he rose again and ascended, and so we are saved.

*How long wilt thou be angry?* ((AUG.)) Wrath passes from the servant, that he may not scourge, as is plain, but that he may not condemn: for wrath endures even toward those converted, but as a wrath that corrects. *For he scourgeth every son whom he receiveth ((Isa. IX, Heb. XII))*.

*Thou wilt feed* ((AUG.)) Here he sets forth the sufferings which the saints are to suffer at the time of the coming. As though he said: Although I long for the coming of Christ, yet at that time we are to suffer many things, because *he fed,* etc. *In measure,* etc. ((AUG.)) According to thy strength, that thou mayest be instructed, not crushed; whence: *God is faithful, who suffereth you not to be tempted above,* etc. ((I Cor. X)). Or, according to the measure of faults.
*Thou hast made us a contradiction.* ((CASS.)) While our neighbours, who are of us, are against us. Our enemies mock us, from all of whom, that we may be saved, *O God of hosts,* etc.
*O God of hosts.* ((AUG.)) It is the way of one who desires, to repeat often what he prays for with such prayers.

*Let thy hand be.* ((CASS.)) A great sacrament, and a gift to God, because the salvation of Israel could be doubted so long, until Christ came: but then the promise was fulfilled, nor does the Church, joined to her spouse, depart from him any more. He says therefore: *Let thy hand be,* he prays for the working of the holy incarnation.
*We depart not.* ((CASS.)) Any more, when *thou shalt quicken* the son of man: this is the profit that comes from him.

*O Lord God of hosts, convert us, show thy face, and we shall be saved.* ((CASS.)) Great is the sweetness of this little verse, in which he sets forth the rule of the whole of religion. For first God *converts* us, and then he shows us *before his face,* that is, he looks upon us with the light of his goodness: after which he at last *saves* us. This verse therefore the prophet repeats, because through it each man briefly implores what is profitable.

notes.text: Always — Whenever I mention you to God in prayer.

In all utterance and knowledge — Of divine things. These gifts the Corinthians particularly admired. Therefore this congratulation naturally tended to soften their spirits, and I make way for the reproofs which follow.

The testimony of Christ — The gospel. Was confirmed among you - By these gifts attending it. They knew they had received these by the hand of Paul: and this consideration was highly proper, to revive in them their former reverence and affection for their spiritual father.
Waiting — With earnest desire. For the glorious Revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ - A sure mark of a true or false Christian, to long for, or dread, this Revelation.

Who will also — if you faithfully apply to him. Confirm you to the end. In the day of Christ - Now it is our day, wherein we are to work out our salvation; then it will be eminently the day of Christ, and of his glory in the saints.
God is faithful — To all his promises; and therefore "to him that hath shall be given." By whom ye are called - A pledge of his willingness to save you unto the uttermost.

glossa.text: *Grace.* First he sets forth what belongs to the good, that others may be conformed to these. *And from the Lord Jesus Christ.* Who is indeed distinguished from the Father by a personal property, but is one God with him by unity of substance.
*In all things.* He subjoins certain particulars, in every word, that is, in every kind of tongues, or in every manner of preaching, that is, to the lesser, the middling, and the perfect.

notes.text: But in those days — Which immediately precede the end of the world: after that tribulation - Above described.
Matt. xxiv, 32; Luke xxi, 28.
He is nigh — The Son of man.
All these things — Relating to the temple and the city.

Of that day — The day of judgment is often in the Scriptures emphatically called that day. Neither the Son - Not as man: as man he was no more omniscient than omnipresent. But as God he knows all the circumstances of it.
Matt. xxiv, 42; Luke xxi, 34.

The Son of man is as a man taking a far journey — Being about to leave this world and go to the Father, he appoints the services that are to be performed by all his servants, in their several stations. This seems chiefly to respect ministers at the day of judgment: but it may be applied to all men, and to the time of death. Matt. xxv, 14; Luke xix, 12.

glossa.text: *But in those days,* etc. ((ID.)) The stars in the judgment shall be seen dark, etc., *as far as* then shall come to pass what the same prophet says elsewhere: *And the light of the moon shall be as the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days ((Isa. III))*.

*Falling down.* From their light, when the seed of Abraham, to which the stars were likened, shall almost fail.

*And the powers which,* etc. ((BEDA.)) What wonder is it that men should tremble, when at the sight of the judgment the angelic powers tremble? Whence Job: *The pillars of heaven tremble, and dread at his beck ((Job. XXVI))*. And what does the little rod of the desert suffer, where the cedar of paradise is shaken? *They shall be moved. ((HIER.))* To the wrath of vengeance, when they shall be sent by the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power, who before came down in humility like rain upon a fleece.

*From the four winds.* From the east and the west, the south, the north, and not only from these; but from the utmost part of the earth to the utmost part of heaven, that is, from the farthest bounds of the earth straight on to its last limits, where to those who look from afar the circle of heaven seems to rest upon the earth.

*But from the fig tree.* As if he said, as when there are tender shoots upon the fig tree, and the bud breaks out into flower, you understand the coming of summer and of spring and of the west wind; so when you shall see these things which are written, think not that the end of the world is already at hand, but that they come as forerunners, to show that it is near.

((BEDA.)) The fig tree is the Synagogue, which, because when the Lord came to her she had not the fruit of justice, etc., *as far as* and the summer of the true light and peace.

((HIER.)) The parable of the fig tree, that is, the prophecy. The leaves that are born are the present words, but the summer near at hand is the day of judgment, in which every tree shall make manifest what it had within, whether dry, for the burning, or green, for the planting in Eden with the tree of life, whose leaves are unto the health of the nations, that is, the words in which it shall be said, *Come, ye blessed of my Father,* etc.

*Heaven and earth shall pass away.* The airy heaven, from which are the birds of heaven and the clouds of heaven, whence Peter: *But the heavens which now are, and the earth, by the same word are laid up in store and reserved unto fire ((II Pet. III))*, plainly teaching that the heavens which are to perish by fire are other than those which were destroyed by water, that is, the empty and cloudy ones. For the water of the flood, which passed the tops of the mountains by fifteen cubits only, did not come beyond the borders of the air and of the ether. Ecclesiastes ((Cap. I)): *One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth standeth for ever.* So therefore heaven and earth pass away according to their image, they remain for ever according to their essence.

*Neither the Son.* -- *For in him are all the treasures of wisdom and of knowledge hidden.* Therefore hidden, because it is not expedient for us to know, whence he says: *It is not for you to know the times or the moments which the Father hath put in his own power ((Act. I))*. In which he shows that he knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that, being always uncertain of the coming of the judge, they may live daily as though they were to be judged on the morrow. The Son therefore knows for himself, but not for us, that we may always be watchful, whence: *see ye, watch,* etc.

((HILAR.)) The Son and the Holy Ghost, because they are not of themselves, do not know of themselves concerning that day: but the Father, because he is of himself, knows of himself.

*And to the porter,* etc. ((HIER.)) To him, namely, who preaches. To whom it is said: *If thou declare not to the wicked man his iniquity, I will require his blood at thy hand ((Ezech. III))*.

*Watch ye therefore.* The example of the father of the household being set before, why he keeps silence about the day of the consummation, he says: *watch ye therefore.* He who sleeps sees not bodies, but phantasms, and when he awakes he has nothing of those things which he had seen. Such are they whom the love of the world snatches away in life, and forsakes after life.

*And what I say to you.* Not only the rulers of the Church, but all of us are bidden to watch, keeping the doors of our hearts; lest the evil suggestion of the ancient enemy steal in, lest the Lord find us sleeping, whence Paul: *Watch, ye just, and sin not.*

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: 'All who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place' reworks Joel's 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved,' transferring the divine Name to Jesus. Volume is high (distinctive idiom 'call on the name'), recurrence strong in Paul (Rom 10:13), and the eschatological-salvation theme coheres tightly with the surrounding 'day of the Lord' language.

echoes.text: and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.’ These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel.”
echoes.note: The address to those 'sanctified... called to be saints' transfers Israel's vocation as a 'holy nation' set apart for God to the Corinthian assembly. The lexical pairing of calling and holiness coheres thematically with the Sinai constitution of a consecrated people; the volume is modest because Paul cites no formula, but the figural availability of Exodus 19 to a Jewish reader is high.

echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
echoes.note: 'Sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints' echoes the Holiness Code refrain 'be holy, for I am holy,' in which Israel's status as God's set-apart people is grounded in God's own holiness. Recurrence is strong across Leviticus 19-20, and the thematic coherence of consecration as gift-and-summons fits Paul's idiom of being made holy in Christ.

echoes.text: It will happen, that he who is left in Zion, and he who remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, even everyone who is written among the living in Jerusalem;
echoes.note: The phrase 'called holy' (kalein hagion) for the eschatological remnant in Zion resonates with 'called to be saints.' The verbal link is suggestive in the LXX, but the volume is faint and the motif is widely diffused, so it is offered only as a contested resonance.

echoes.text: A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The idiom 'call on the name of the LORD' first appears at the dawn of worship in Genesis 4:26 and runs through the patriarchal narratives (Gen 12:8; 13:4). It supplies the deep semantic background for Paul's phrase, though Joel is the proximate and more specific source.

echoes.text: I will take the cup of salvation, and call on Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The cultic act of 'calling on the name of the LORD' in the thanksgiving psalter underlies the worship-language of 'all who call on the name.' Recurrence within the Psalms is notable, but the volume here is faint relative to the Joel allusion that controls the phrase.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: Zephaniah's promise that the nations will 'call on the name of the LORD' with one accord matches Paul's universalizing 'in every place, both theirs and ours.' The thematic coherence of an ingathered people invoking the Name is good, but the verbal contact is light and the motif overlaps with Joel.

echoes.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light.
echoes.note: The repeated 'day of our Lord Jesus Christ' (v.8) draws on the prophetic 'day of the LORD' tradition, of which Amos is the classic warning text. Thematic coherence is strong: Paul reframes the eschatological day as the point of vindication 'blameless,' and the recurrence of yom YHWH across the prophets gives the motif high availability.

echoes.text: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'The day of our Lord' as the eschatological revelation aligns with Joel's 'great and terrible day of the LORD,' the same chapter Paul has just drawn on in v.2. The internal recurrence (Joel within the immediate context) strengthens the case for a Joel-shaped horizon, though the phrase is generic enough to be merely traditional.

echoes.text: Know therefore that Yahweh your God himself is God, the faithful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with them who love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations,
echoes.note: 'God is faithful, through whom you were called' (v.9) echoes the covenant formula that 'the LORD your God is the faithful God who keeps covenant.' Volume is good on the distinctive predicate 'faithful' applied to God as the guarantor of a calling, and the covenant-keeping theme coheres with Paul's assurance of preservation to the end.

echoes.text: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly.
echoes.note: Zephaniah's 'great day of the LORD is near' is among the most concentrated 'day of the LORD' oracles and feeds the same prophetic reservoir behind v.8. The volume is low because Paul names no specific feature of Zephaniah's day, but the motif's availability is high.

echoes.text: “But who can endure the day of his coming? And who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire, and like launderer’s soap;
echoes.note: 'Who can stand when he appears?'—the day that tests and refines—coheres with Paul's hope that the Corinthians be 'confirmed... blameless in the day.' The forensic-purgative coloring of being found unblamable resonates, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are just. A God of faithfulness who does no wrong, just and right is he.
echoes.note: The Song of Moses names God 'faithful (pistos) and without iniquity,' a likely LXX source for Paul's 'God is faithful.' Recurrence of the divine epithet pistos in Deuteronomy supports availability, though the phrase had become a settled liturgical commonplace.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine.
echoes.note: 'The sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light' is near-verbatim from Isaiah 13:10, 'the sun will be dark at its rising and the moon will not shed its light,' the day-of-the-LORD oracle against Babylon. The catastrophic dimming of the luminaries is the lead element of Mark's cosmic-collapse cluster; highest volume in the constellation.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: 'The stars will be falling from heaven and the powers of the heavens will be shaken' draws on Isaiah 34:4, 'all the host of heaven shall rot away, the skies roll up like a scroll, all their host fall.' Mark's falling stars and shaken heavenly powers reproduce Isaiah's cosmic-judgment imagery (LXX 'the powers of the heavens shall melt').

echoes.text: The earth quakes before them. The heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.
echoes.note: 'The sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining' (also 2:31, 3:15) is a primary source for Mark's three-element luminary collapse. Joel's day-of-the-LORD theophany combines earth-quaking, heaven-trembling, and darkened sun/moon/stars, matching Mark's whole cluster and reinforcing the multiply-attested character of the imagery.

echoes.text: When I shall extinguish you, I will cover the heavens, and make its stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of the sky will I make dark over you, and set darkness on your land, says the Lord Yahweh.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's lament over Pharaoh: 'I will cover the heavens and darken their stars; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven I will darken,' supplies the exact 'moon shall not give its light' phrase Mark shares with Isaiah 13. A fourth witness in the darkening cluster, demonstrating Hays' recurrence.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: 'They will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory' directly cites Daniel 7:13, 'one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven.' This is the christological centerpiece of the discourse; Mark adds 'power and glory' from the dominion granted in 7:14, and the title 'Son of Man' is the load-bearing self-designation throughout Mark.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'With great power and glory' renders the gift to the son of man of 'dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples should serve him.' Mark fuses 7:13's coming-on-clouds with 7:14's enthronement glory, so the Son of Man's parousia carries the universal dominion of Daniel's vision.

echoes.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says Yahweh; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Gather the elect from the four winds' echoes Zechariah 2:6, 'I have spread you abroad as the four winds of heaven, declares the LORD,' a regathering-of-the-dispersed oracle. The eschatological ingathering of the scattered people from the four winds is the conceptual core of Mark's angelic harvest of the elect.

echoes.text: If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of the heavens, from there Yahweh your God will gather you, and from there he will bring you back.
echoes.note: 'If your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the LORD will gather you' undergirds gathering the elect 'from the ends of the earth to the ends of the sky.' Deuteronomy's covenant promise of regathering the exiled from the extremities of earth and heaven matches Mark's double horizon precisely.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: Isaiah's promise that the LORD will 'assemble the banished of Israel and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth' supplies the messianic-age ingathering behind Mark's gathering of the elect. The 'four corners/four winds' regathering is a recurrent restoration motif, here applied to the Son of Man's harvest.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that a great trumpet will be blown; and those who were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and those who were outcasts in the land of Egypt, shall come; and they will worship Yahweh in the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
echoes.note: 'A great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost... will come and worship the LORD' from the Isaiah Apocalypse provides the trumpet-summoned ingathering of the scattered; Matthew's parallel makes the trumpet explicit. Mark's angelic gathering coheres with this Isaianic regathering even without naming the trumpet.

echoes.text: I will pour on the house of David, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son, and will grieve bitterly for him, as one grieves for his firstborn. In that day there will be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. The land will mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of […]
echoes.note: 'They will look on him whom they have pierced' and the mourning of the tribes lies behind 'they will see the Son of Man'; the seeing-and-mourning at the coming one is more explicit in Matthew 24:30 and Revelation 1:7 but may color Mark's 'they will see.' Faint in Mark, marked contested.
echoes.lxxText: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and compassion: and they shall look upon me, because they have mocked me, and they shall make lamentation for him, as for a beloved friend, and they shall grieve intensely, as for a firstborn son. In that day the lamentation in Jerusalem shall be very great, as the mourning for the pomegranate grove cut down in the plain. And the land shall lament in separate families, the […]

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' parallels the Son of Man sending out his angels at the parousia. The accompanying-holy-ones motif of the day of the LORD coheres with Mark's angelic retinue; included for recurrence of the Zecharianic day-of-the-LORD material in this pericope.

echoes.text: He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters. He makes the clouds his chariot. He walks on the wings of the wind.
echoes.note: 'He makes the clouds his chariot, riding on the wings of the wind' is part of the OT cloud-rider theophany tradition (cf. Isaiah 19:1; Psalm 18:9-12) that informs the Son of Man's coming 'in clouds.' The divine-prerogative of cloud-borne arrival lends figural weight to Daniel 7's cloud-coming as Mark applies it.

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look on the earth beneath; for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment; and those who dwell therein shall die in the same way: but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not be abolished.
echoes.note: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away' draws on Isaiah 51:6, 'the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth wear out like a garment... but my salvation will be forever.' The contrast between the perishing cosmos and the enduring divine word is distinctively Isaianic and high in volume.

echoes.text: The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever' is the closest source for the permanence of God's word over against transient creation. Mark transfers the abiding-word of Isaiah 40 to 'my words,' an implicit christological claim; the verbal contrast (pass away / not pass away vs. wither / stand forever) is strong.

echoes.text: Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same. Your years will have no end.
echoes.note: 'They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment... but you are the same' grounds 'heaven and earth will pass away.' The Psalm's contrast of the perishable heavens-and-earth with the unchanging LORD supplies the theological warrant Mark applies to the abiding word.

echoes.text: Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.
echoes.note: The fig-tree parable ('the fig tree puts forth... you know summer is near') faintly recalls Joel's restoration imagery, 'the fig tree and vine give their full yield,' as a sign-bearing tree marking the season's turn. The fig tree elsewhere in Mark (11:13-21) carries judgment symbolism; here its budding signals nearness, a season-discernment topos. Contested.

echoes.text: All of the army of the sky will be dissolved. The sky will be rolled up like a scroll, and all its armies will fade away, as a leaf fades from off a vine or a fig tree.
echoes.note: 'All the host of heaven shall rot away and the skies roll up like a scroll' reinforces 'heaven and earth will pass away,' connecting this declaration to the cosmic-dissolution imagery already cited at 13:25. Recurrence of Isaiah 34 across the discourse supports its faint presence here.

echoes.text: But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.
echoes.note: 'All these things' coming to pass before 'this generation' passes resonates with Daniel's assurance that 'the saints shall receive the kingdom... forever, forever and ever'; the certainty that the decreed events will be accomplished is Danielic. Faint, included for the apocalyptic guarantee that frames 'most certainly I say.'

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished. I heard, but I didn’t understand: then I said, my lord, what shall be the issue of these things? He said, Go your way, […]
echoes.note: Daniel is told 'the words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end' — the timing of the consummation is withheld even from the seer. Mark's 'no one knows the day or hour' continues this Danielic concealment of the appointed time, the necessary counterpart to the timetable expounded throughout the chapter.

echoes.text: I will stand at my watch, and set myself on the ramparts, and will look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint. Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it. For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: The watchman who stations himself to keep watch (2:1) and the vision that 'awaits its appointed time... if it seems slow, wait for it' (2:3) supplies the watching-for-a-delayed-coming posture behind the doorkeeper commanded to keep watch and the repeated 'watch.' The waiting-watchman for an appointed-yet-delayed arrival is the Habakkuk pattern.

echoes.text: For the Lord said to me, “Go, set a watchman. Let him declare what he sees. When he sees a troop, horsemen in pairs, a troop of donkeys, a troop of camels, he shall listen diligently with great attentiveness.” He cried like a lion: “Lord, I stand continually on the watchtower in the daytime, and every night I stay at my post.
echoes.note: 'Go, set a watchman... he calls, Upon a watchtower I stand continually by day, and at my post whole nights' provides the prophetic figure of the sentinel keeping watch through the night-watches. Mark's doorkeeper told to 'keep watch' and the listing of evening/midnight/cockcrow/morning watches draw on this watchman tradition.

echoes.text: It will be a unique day which is known to Yahweh; not day, and not night; but it will come to pass, that at evening time there will be light.
echoes.note: 'A unique day... known to the LORD' on which the timing is hidden faintly parallels 'of that day or hour no one knows... but only the Father.' Zechariah's day-of-the-LORD whose timing belongs to God alone coheres with Mark's reservation of the hour to the Father; contested.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple' parallels the master who returns 'suddenly,' lest he find the servants sleeping. The sudden, unannounced arrival of the lord coheres with Malachi's suddenly-coming Lord; faint and contested, but Malachi is a recurrent source in Mark.

echoes.text: Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and tell them, When I bring the sword on a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and set him for their watchman; if, when he sees the sword come on the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people; then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, and doesn’t take warning, if the sword come, and take him away, his blood shall be on his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet, and […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's watchman charged with sounding the alarm and held accountable if he fails to keep watch supplies the responsibility-of-the-sentinel theme behind 'commanded the doorkeeper to keep watch.' Faint relative to Isaiah 21 and Habakkuk 2; included for the recurrent watchman motif.

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.
echoes.note: The parable of the man who goes abroad, leaves his house, and assigns each servant authority over his work faintly recalls the trusted-steward-over-an-absent-master's-household pattern (e.g., Joseph over Potiphar's house). A diffuse OT household-management topos rather than a specific text; low confidence.

echoes.text: in the twilight, in the evening of the day, in the middle of the night and in the darkness. Behold, there a woman met him with the attire of a prostitute, and with crafty intent.
echoes.note: The four night-watches (evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning) draw on the OT/Second-Temple reckoning of the night's divisions; Proverbs' 'in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness' attests the watch-segmented night. Marked contested as a cultural-temporal echo rather than a quoted text.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Tear open the heavens and come down.
Stir up your power, O God, and save us.
The fig tree softens; summer is near.
We watch for the Son of Man in the clouds.
Keep awake — you do not know the hour.
We are watching. Come, Lord Jesus.
Come, let us worship the God who is near.
We come, awake and waiting. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: It is the dark before morning, and we are keeping watch — the lamp trimmed, the door unlatched, our eyes on the eastern sky.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
You tore open the heavens once and came down; the mountains shook to know you near. Tear them open again.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
We have waited through the long evening, through the midnight and the cockcrow, and we will not sleep.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
So we gather in the dark and keep the watch together, sure that the dawn belongs to you.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The night is long; we keep the lamp burning.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Tear open the heavens; let your face shine.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Keep us awake until the morning breaks.
Come, Lord Jesus, come.
Come, let us worship and watch for the dawn.
Come, Lord Jesus, come. Amen.
